title: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 21 (Authentication of documents, proceedings and contracts)

content.overview: Section 21 permits a company document or proceeding requiring authentication, and contracts made by or on behalf of the company, to be signed by a key managerial personnel or an officer/employee duly authorised by the Board, subject to the Act.
content.glance: Authentication and company contracts may be signed by authorised key managerial personnel or an authorised officer/employee, subject to the Act.
content.study: Section 21 establishes an internal authority rule for authentication and contracting. Unless the Companies Act provides otherwise, a document or proceeding requiring authentication by a company, and contracts made by or on behalf of a company, may be signed by any key managerial personnel or an officer or employee of the company duly authorised by the Board. The analysis should therefore identify the document or contract, the signatory's status, the Board's authority, and any contrary provision in the Act.

sections.heading: Scope
sections.body: The section applies, subject to other provisions of the Act, to documents or proceedings requiring company authentication and to contracts made by or on behalf of the company.

sections.heading: Authorised signatory
sections.body: The permitted signatory is a key managerial personnel or an officer/employee of the company who has been duly authorised by the Board.

sections.heading: Board authorisation
sections.body: For an officer or employee who is not signing merely in a qualifying KMP capacity, the Board authorisation is a material authority fact to establish.

sections.heading: Application test
sections.body: Check the nature of the instrument, statutory exceptions, signatory capacity and Board authorisation before treating the signature as company authentication or execution.

cases.name: Salomon v. A. Salomon & Co. Ltd.
cases.facts: A properly incorporated company was challenged as indistinct from its controlling shareholder.
cases.issue: What is the legal effect of incorporation?
cases.ratioDecidendi: A registered company is a legal person separate from its members, even when control and ownership are concentrated.
cases.holding: The company's separate personality was affirmed.
cases.relevance: Use for Companies Act s. 9 and corporate personality.

cases.name: Foss v. Harbottle
cases.facts: Shareholders sought relief for alleged wrongs to the company.
cases.issue: Who may sue for a wrong done to the company and when may exceptions apply?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The company is the proper plaintiff for corporate wrongs, subject to recognised exceptions such as fraud on the minority and ultra vires acts.
cases.holding: The proper-plaintiff and majority-rule principles were established.
cases.relevance: Use with oppression, mismanagement and class-action analysis.

cases.name: Needle Industries (India) Ltd. v. Needle Industries Newey (India) Holding Ltd.
cases.facts: The Court examined share issue powers and alleged oppression.
cases.issue: When does a corporate action become oppressive or invalid?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The Court examines purpose, fairness, statutory power and resulting prejudice rather than treating every irregularity as oppression.
cases.holding: The corporate action was assessed under the statutory and equitable framework.
cases.relevance: Use for share allotment and oppression claims.

cases.name: Miheer H. Mafatlal v. Mafatlal Industries Ltd.
cases.facts: The Court reviewed a scheme of arrangement sanctioned by the company court.
cases.issue: What is the court's role in sanctioning a corporate scheme?
cases.ratioDecidendi: The court must ensure statutory compliance, class fairness, informed approval and absence of illegality, but does not substitute its commercial judgment for the company's decision.
cases.holding: The principles governing scheme sanction were stated.
cases.relevance: Use for corporate arrangements and tribunal scrutiny.

enhancement.detailedExplanation:
Section 21 establishes an internal authority rule for authentication and contracting. Unless the Companies Act provides otherwise, a document or proceeding requiring authentication by a company, and contracts made by or on behalf of a company, may be signed by any key managerial personnel or an officer or employee of the company duly authorised by the Board. The analysis should therefore identify the document or contract, the signatory's status, the Board's authority, and any contrary provision in the Act.

Key statutory components:
1. Scope — The section applies, subject to other provisions of the Act, to documents or proceedings requiring company authentication and to contracts made by or on behalf of the company.
2. Authorised signatory — The permitted signatory is a key managerial personnel or an officer/employee of the company who has been duly authorised by the Board.
3. Board authorisation — For an officer or employee who is not signing merely in a qualifying KMP capacity, the Board authorisation is a material authority fact to establish.
4. Application test — Check the nature of the instrument, statutory exceptions, signatory capacity and Board authorisation before treating the signature as company authentication or execution.
